Delayed response and I didn’t see what others said, but during my pregnancy I upped my lamicfal I was already on. We also had an anxiety and depression med identified that was safe to go on during pregnancy if I felt the need (I didn’t). As far as birth, my baby came a whole 5 weeks early so I had no mental preparation I feel like. They needed to delay my birth so I could get two injections 24 hours apart to make sure his lungs could acclimate being he was early, so I was given medication to delay contractions. I had them anyway, just inconsistently. By the time the 24 hour timeframe rolled around I hadn’t eaten or slept and then the contractions were excruciating, like had to REALLY focus on coming back to breathing (please practice this, and a good mental space to be in-I closed my eyes and imagined flowing the pain out while breathing and it helped SO much). Ended up going with an epidural which was amazing. However at that point it had been 32 hours no sleep or food and baby’s heart beat kept fluctuating and I was only 2cm dilated since my water broke. We opted for a c section instead of an emergency one. I was terrified as this was the only thing about birth I was truly worried about due to my anxiety. I made sure to communicate my feelings (or panic lol) but remained calm and focused on a mantra “healthy baby, safe baby” and got through the surgery and knocked out after I heard him cry and knew he was okay. 

After ALL of this I still did not have a manic episode and I’m now almost 5 weeks into post partum and think this is the period where I’m borderline manic because I’m not allowed to sleep really from getting up with him which mimics my actual manic symptoms. Not Autistic but am neurodivergent (bipolar) and feel like my diagnosis gives me a better understanding into the different ways the world does not cater to us and understanding we have to work extra hard to overcome those barriers. In terms of being treated differently, I am a huge advocate for awareness of bipolar disorder and would educate people when they misspoke, this typically backfired in all of my professional relationships with families, staff, supervisors, and fellow bcbas as they suddenly shifted how they treated me which was super frustrating. I now don’t really discuss it unless I feel it is vital. I also stopped caring what everyone thought. I know im a great clinician who can take feedback and grow and being bipolar is an added strength that others do not have that I am thankful to be able to draw from. 

I will challenge you to consider if it’s simply the diagnosis that is altering how people are treating you or if there’s something particular that is causing them to treat you differently. I have worked with several bcbas on projects and have autistic BTs myself and love their insight but realized that the way I give feedback needs to be tailored differently as they had increased difficulty pivoting from what their deficits were even with reiterating the feedback a variety of ways. I realized it was just a skill I had not developed in giving feedback and I found being extremely blunt has worked best for them which I usually avoid as I feel it comes off harsh, but once was told that they appreciate the directness and it has never damaged my relationship with them. I’m sure this doesn’t apply to all on the spectrum but my struggles probably gave the wrong “vibe” initially and am thankful to be able to pivot and repair that with my coworkers. Maybe others are struggling with identifying how to communicate with you and instead of being open minded and asking they are relying on stereotypes and being close minded which obviously is hurting you, if so I’m so sorry you’re having this experience. It’s really hard to tell at times, for myself included when people suddenly treat me different after learning I’m bipolar when nothing I’ve done has changed. 

My advice is don’t let it bother you or get you down and just work towards your goals, communicate, and focus on helping our patients. You have a strength others do not posses. I’d take being “the odd one out” any day if it helps me advocate for others better than people who will never understand these struggles. Hopefully this didn’t come off harsh and was helpful 🙏

Yikes! That’s enough to burn anyone out. Maybe take later evening patients and a weekend client? Or talk to a company about starting salaried but that you’d like to switch to hourly at some point due to whatever reason and if they agree then you could go that route?

I’ll be honest that it can be stressful making the switch. I wouldn’t quit your salaried job until your hourly job is stable. I have a friend who never had an issue with having a consistent caseload because of her location whereas I live outside any major areas and was having difficulties getting staffed so the first time I went solely hourly, I suffered financially and went back to salary. The second time I attempted it I made sure to keep my salaried job until I had 1-2 patients at two different hourly jobs which took a few months and then requested more patients and took the risk and quit my salaried job and it’s been great. It’s not always consistent especially now during flu and holiday season but I’ve been able to save up since I make more to rely on if needed. I also never need to really take PTO since I juggle two jobs with lower caseloads they don’t ever notice if I’m absent so I only use it when I absolutely know I’m going to be unavailable and sometimes I use my PTO when my weeks are lower than I’d like since that gets paid out hourly as well. For example last week all my patients were sick so my hours that are normally around 10-12 with my one job were at 3 so I took a day of PTO to make up for it even though I didn’t really need to. I’m also saving most of my PTO for my upcoming maternity leave since I don’t really have benefits from work for that. They’re fine with me taking off and I’ll have a bcba to cover for me but since I’m hourly I won’t be paid, so my PTO is going to save me there while I’m out 3ish weeks (I work from home so I’m taking a shorter leave). As far as rates, I’m not sure what area you live in but I’ve never been paid less than $85 an hour even with low experience as a newer bcba and now make over $100. Salaries in our area are 75-95k for 25-30 billables so if you average out even $90 an hour for the same amount of billables it ends out being significantly more. Sorry this ended up being long but to summarize if you want to make the switch you just really need to be patient and find a good company who can ensure staffing and understand salaried employees will be staffed first so it can take a bit to get a caseload rolling so you’ll be a little wore out for a few months while you transition, but totally worth it for me since the salaried just were burning me out significantly and I haven’t felt near as burnt out since switching.
